```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
backends <- attribute_truth_backends()
crowdkit_available <- isTRUE(backends$available[backends$backend == "crowd_kit"])
```

The other vignettes in this package each demonstrate one comparison at a time. This one asks
a different question: on a *single* panel, built once, how many genuinely different ways can
these sources be compared -- timing, agreement, staleness, volatility, coverage, convergence,
independence, and weight -- and what does each one actually add that the others don't?

**The panel below is simulated, not real.** Real per-NPI midwifery data cannot appear in this
package (see "What this vignette does and does not show"). It is *calibrated* to the real,
already-published findings this package's other docs establish -- the disagreement rates, lag
patterns, and reliability rankings below are chosen to land in the same neighborhood as the
real numbers, not to reproduce them exactly. Every real number cited is explicitly marked as
such and sourced to its doc.

## Building one panel, once

Four simulated sources, 250 synthetic clinicians (`"S0001"`-`"S0250"`, never real NPIs), 2017-2024,
state-level only:

- **NPPES** -- the reference panel. State changes ("moves") happen at a baseline 7%/year rate,
  elevated to 16% for the 2017-to-2018 and 2023-to-2024 transitions specifically -- the same two
  transitions `docs/midwifery-ablation-findings.md` and `docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md`
  identify as real migration spikes in the actual cohort.
- **DAC and PECOS** (raw, separate) -- each lags NPPES, with its own independent noise on top.
  Rural clinicians' records lag 4 years; urban clinicians' lag 1 year -- a deliberate, calibrated
  covariate effect (see Agreement, below), not sampling noise. Combined via
  `attribute_claims_collapse_lineage()` below, same as the real project's `dac_pecos_combined`.
- **Open Payments** -- sparse (~25% of entity-years), calibrated to the real cohort's observed
  ~23% coverage (`docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md` S2: 807 of 3,556 touched NPI-years).
- **T-MSIS** (Medicaid enrollment) -- moderate coverage (~65%), but only ~50% agreement with
  NPPES when both are present -- calibrated directly to the real, verified finding that T-MSIS
  agreed with NPPES only 50.3% of the time (`docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md` S2).

```{r build-panel}
set.seed(20261106)
n <- 250L
ids <- sprintf("S%04d", seq_len(n))
years <- 2017:2024
states <- c("CO", "NM", "TX", "NY", "CA", "WA", "OH", "GA")

move_prob <- setNames(rep(0.07, length(years) - 1), paste0(years[-length(years)], "-", years[-1]))
move_prob["2017-2018"] <- 0.16
move_prob["2023-2024"] <- 0.16

truth <- matrix(NA_character_, n, length(years))
truth[, 1] <- sample(states, n, replace = TRUE)
for (k in 2:length(years)) {
  p <- move_prob[paste0(years[k - 1], "-", years[k])]
  moved <- runif(n) < p
  truth[, k] <- truth[, k - 1]
  truth[moved, k] <- sapply(truth[moved, k - 1], function(s) sample(setdiff(states, s), 1))
}

practice_setting <- sample(c("rural", "urban"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.7))
lag_vec <- ifelse(practice_setting == "rural", 4L, 1L) # deliberate covariate effect
noise_p <- 0.15

make_dac_pecos_source <- function() {
  m <- matrix(NA_character_, n, length(years)); m[, 1] <- truth[, 1]
  for (k in 2:length(years)) {
    lag_idx <- pmax(1L, k - lag_vec)
    m[, k] <- truth[cbind(seq_len(n), lag_idx)]
    noisy <- runif(n) < noise_p
    m[noisy, k] <- sapply(m[noisy, k - 1], function(s) sample(setdiff(states, s), 1))
  }
  m
}
dac_raw <- make_dac_pecos_source()
pecos_raw <- make_dac_pecos_source()

op_present <- matrix(runif(n * length(years)) < 0.25, n, length(years))
op <- matrix(NA_character_, n, length(years)); op[op_present] <- truth[op_present]

tmsis_present <- matrix(runif(n * length(years)) < 0.65, n, length(years))
tmsis <- matrix(NA_character_, n, length(years))
agree_mask <- tmsis_present & (matrix(runif(n * length(years)), n, length(years)) < 0.50)
tmsis[agree_mask] <- truth[agree_mask]
disagree_mask <- tmsis_present & !agree_mask
tmsis[disagree_mask] <- sapply(truth[disagree_mask], function(s) sample(setdiff(states, s), 1))

to_long <- function(mat) {
  df <- data.frame(npi = rep(ids, times = length(years)), year = rep(years, each = n),
                    state = as.vector(mat), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  df[!is.na(df$state), , drop = FALSE]
}
nppes <- to_long(truth)
dac_raw_long <- to_long(dac_raw)
pecos_raw_long <- to_long(pecos_raw)
open_payments <- to_long(op)
tmsis_long <- to_long(tmsis)
c(nppes = nrow(nppes), dac = nrow(dac_raw_long), pecos = nrow(pecos_raw_long),
  open_payments = nrow(open_payments), tmsis = nrow(tmsis_long))
```

## Independence: merging DAC and PECOS before they count as two votes

DAC and PECOS share CMS/PECOS enrollment lineage in the real data
(`docs/midwifery-ablation-findings.md` S1) -- here they're deliberately *built* that way, both
derived from the same `truth` matrix. `attribute_claims_collapse_lineage()` is the general form
of the "agree -> one vote; disagree -> no vote; one present -> use it" rule the real project's
claims table already used:

```{r collapse-lineage}
to_claims <- function(df, source_name) {
  transform(df, entity_id = npi, attribute = "practice_state", source_id = source_name,
            claimed_value = state, reference_year = year)[
              , c("entity_id", "attribute", "source_id", "claimed_value", "reference_year")]
}
claims_dac_pecos <- rbind(to_claims(dac_raw_long, "dac"), to_claims(pecos_raw_long, "pecos"))
collapsed <- attribute_claims_collapse_lineage(
  claims_dac_pecos, lineage_groups = list(dac_pecos_combined = c("dac", "pecos"))
)
attr(collapsed, "report")

dac_pecos_combined <- collapsed[collapsed$source_id == "dac_pecos_combined",
                                  c("entity_id", "claimed_value", "reference_year")]
names(dac_pecos_combined) <- c("npi", "state", "year")
```

DAC and PECOS disagree on about a quarter of the entity-years where both have a claim (the
`entity_attribute_years_dropped_conflict` count above) -- close to the real cohort's own
26.6% DAC/PECOS disagreement rate despite shared lineage
(`docs/midwifery-ablation-findings.md` S1), even though these two sources were built from one
shared `truth` matrix by construction. Shared lineage does not mean the two copies agree.

## Timing: who moves first, how often it resolves, how long it takes

```{r timing}
ll <- attribute_lead_lag_matrix(nppes, dac_pecos_combined, attributes = "state", base_year = 2019L)
as.data.frame(ll)[, c("a_breaks_concordance_first", "b_breaks_concordance_first",
                        "n_discordant_at_t", "b_adopts_a_at_t1_pct",
                        "disc_base_n", "b_adopts_a_multi_pct", "a_reverts_b_multi_pct")]

dur <- attribute_lead_lag_duration(
  nppes, dac_pecos_combined, attribute = "state", base_year = 2019L,
  source_a_label = "NPPES", source_b_label = "DAC/PECOS"
)
dur$combined_text
```

Three distinct timing questions, three distinct answers: **direction** -- NPPES breaks
concordance first far more often than DAC/PECOS does (`a_breaks_concordance_first` far exceeds
`b_breaks_concordance_first`), consistent with DAC/PECOS being the lagging copy by construction.
**How often it resolves** -- of the identifiers disagreeing with NPPES in 2019, the large
majority of DAC/PECOS's eventual matches do happen (`b_adopts_a_multi_pct`), while NPPES almost
never reverts to DAC/PECOS's version. **How long it takes** -- `attribute_lead_lag_duration()`
adds the piece neither of the above states: a *median* number of years until that adoption
actually happens, pulled up by the rural clinicians' 4-year lag mixed in with the urban
clinicians' 1-year lag.

## Agreement: do they say the same thing, and does that depend on who you ask

```{r agreement}
agr <- attribute_agreement(list(nppes = nppes, dac_pecos = dac_pecos_combined), attribute = "state")
agr_summary <- attribute_agreement_summary(agr)
as.data.frame(agr_summary)[, c("year", "n_compared", "n_agree", "pct_agree")]

wilson_ci(sum(agr$agree), nrow(agr), as_percent = TRUE)
```

Overall agreement, with a Wilson interval the same way every proportion in this package's docs
is reported -- but a single pooled number hides the covariate effect built into this panel on
purpose:

```{r agreement-covariate}
nppes_2024 <- nppes[nppes$year == 2024, c("npi", "state")]
dac_2024 <- dac_pecos_combined[dac_pecos_combined$year == 2024, c("npi", "state")]
covdf <- data.frame(npi = ids, setting = practice_setting)
abc <- attribute_agreement_by_covariate(
  nppes_2024, dac_2024, covdf, attribute = "state", covariate = "setting",
  comparison_label = "NPPES vs DAC/PECOS (2024)"
)
as.data.frame(abc)
```

Rural clinicians' DAC/PECOS records agree with NPPES noticeably less often than urban
clinicians' -- exactly the 4-year-vs-1-year lag built into the panel, made visible only by
stratifying. The pooled 2024 agreement rate alone would never have surfaced this; it is the
point of `attribute_agreement_by_covariate()` and `attribute_agreement_by_spell_age()`
(demonstrated on a different panel in `vignette("lead-lag-staleness")`) specifically.

## Staleness: how long has a value sat unchanged

```{r staleness}
sa <- attribute_spell_age(nppes, attribute = "state")
table(sa$spell_age_years)
```

Most NPPES entity-years have a spell age of 0-2 years (the value was set recently, or the panel
itself is young at that point), with a long tail out to 7 years for clinicians whose state
never changed across the whole simulated panel. `classify_record_staleness()` and
`record_age_years()`/`record_age_band()` answer a related but distinct question -- given two
records' own *last-updated dates* (not panel years), which one is provably older information --
demonstrated in full in `vignette("attribute-agreement")`, not repeated here since this panel
has no per-record update timestamps to show it with.

## Volatility/churn: how often a source's own value flips, regardless of direction

```{r churn}
churn_nppes <- attribute_churn_rate(nppes, attribute = "state")
churn_tmsis <- attribute_churn_rate(tmsis_long, attribute = "state")
c(nppes_churn_pct = churn_nppes$overall$pct, tmsis_churn_pct = churn_tmsis$overall$pct)

format_proportion_comparison_prose(
  n_a = churn_nppes$overall$n_changed, n_total_a = churn_nppes$overall$n_transitions,
  n_b = churn_tmsis$overall$n_changed, n_total_b = churn_tmsis$overall$n_transitions,
  label_a = "NPPES", label_b = "T-MSIS",
  unit_label = "consecutive-year transitions", condition_label = "showed a changed state"
)$comparison_sentence
```

```{r fig-churn, fig.alt = "Grouped bar chart comparing NPPES and T-MSIS churn rate: NPPES changes state in roughly 9 percent of consecutive-year transitions, T-MSIS in roughly 70 percent."}
churn_tbl <- c(NPPES = churn_nppes$overall$pct, `T-MSIS` = churn_tmsis$overall$pct)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
mid <- barplot(churn_tbl, col = c("#1F2A33", "#C8553D"), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 1,
               ylab = "% of transitions with a changed value",
               main = "Churn rate: how often does each source's own value flip?", cex.main = 1)
text(mid, churn_tbl, sprintf("%.1f%%", churn_tbl), pos = 3)
par(op)
```

T-MSIS changes its reported state on roughly 70% of consecutive-year transitions, versus
roughly 9% for NPPES -- a dramatic, highly significant difference, and notably this says
nothing yet about which one is *right*. It says T-MSIS is simply far less stable, which is
itself informative: a source that flips this often is a weak foundation for inferring a real
move, independent of the ~50% NPPES-agreement rate already established for the real T-MSIS data.

## Coverage: which source actually has data for more entity-years

```{r coverage}
universe <- unique(nppes[, c("npi", "year")])
cov <- attribute_coverage(
  list(nppes = nppes, dac_pecos_combined = dac_pecos_combined,
       open_payments = open_payments, tmsis = tmsis_long),
  attribute = "state", universe = universe
)
as.data.frame(cov$overall)

format_ranking_prose(
  group = cov$overall$source, value = cov$overall$pct, n = cov$overall$n_total,
  value_label = "coverage of the NPPES universe", fmt = "%.1f", suffix = "%"
)$sentence
```

```{r fig-coverage, fig.alt = "Bar chart ranking four sources by percent coverage of the NPPES universe of entity-years: NPPES 100 percent, DAC/PECOS about 77 percent, T-MSIS about 63 percent, Open Payments about 25 percent."}
cov_tbl <- setNames(cov$overall$pct, cov$overall$source)
op <- par(mar = c(7, 4, 3, 1))
barplot(cov_tbl, col = "#8AA29E", border = NA, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 2,
        ylab = "% of universe entity-years covered",
        main = "Coverage: which source actually has the data?", cex.main = 1)
par(op)
```

T-MSIS and Open Payments both rank low on coverage *and* (for T-MSIS) high on churn -- two
separate limitations that compound: T-MSIS is both less complete and less stable than NPPES or
DAC/PECOS, not just one or the other. Open Payments is the sparsest (~25% of entity-years,
matching the real cohort's own ~23% figure cited above) but, as the next section shows, is not
thereby the least trustworthy of what it does cover.

## Convergence: which source does everyone else trust, and who's the outlier

```{r convergence}
corrob <- attribute_source_corroboration(
  list(nppes = nppes, dac_pecos = dac_pecos_combined, open_payments = open_payments, tmsis = tmsis_long),
  attributes = "state"
)
as.data.frame(corrob)[, c("source", "led_n", "corrected_n", "opportunities_n", "lead_rate")]

format_ranking_prose(
  group = corrob$source, value = 100 * corrob$lead_rate, n = corrob$opportunities_n,
  value_label = "lead rate (how often the ecosystem converges toward this source)",
  fmt = "%.1f", suffix = "%"
)$sentence

ooo <- attribute_odd_one_out(
  list(nppes = nppes, dac_pecos = dac_pecos_combined, open_payments = open_payments, tmsis = tmsis_long),
  attribute = "state"
)
ooo_rate <- attribute_odd_one_out_rate(ooo)
as.data.frame(ooo_rate)

format_ranking_prose(
  group = ooo_rate$source, value = 100 * ooo_rate$odd_rate, n = ooo_rate$n_eligible,
  value_label = "odd-one-out rate", fmt = "%.1f", suffix = "%"
)$sentence
```

T-MSIS has by far the lowest `lead_rate` -- other sources essentially never converge toward
its value after a disagreement -- and by far the highest odd-one-out rate, meaning when 3+
sources disagree, T-MSIS is disproportionately the lone dissenter rather than part of a
contested pair. Open Payments, despite covering the fewest entity-years, has a *high* lead
rate on the ones it does cover: a reminder from this function's own documentation that "a
source that leads is informative; a source that never leads is not thereby correct." Sparse
and trusted are not opposites.

`format_ranking_prose()`'s lead-rate sentence also did something worth noticing on its own:
it flagged `dac_pecos` and `open_payments` as **tied** at 100.0% rather than silently picking
one to list first. Both genuinely display the same rounded value here -- exactly the case this
function exists to catch rather than hide behind an arbitrary `order()` tie-break.

## Weight: when a method is forced to pick one value

```{r weight}
claims_all <- rbind(
  to_claims(nppes, "nppes"), to_claims(dac_pecos_combined, "dac_pecos_combined"),
  to_claims(open_payments, "open_payments"), to_claims(tmsis_long, "tmsis")
)
maj <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims_all, method = "majority")
attribute_truth_fusion_prose(maj, result_label = "the simulated panel")$combined_text
```

```{r weight-ds, eval = crowdkit_available}
ds <- suppressWarnings(attribute_truth_fusion(claims_all, method = "dawid_skene"))
attribute_truth_fusion_prose(ds, result_label = "the simulated panel")$reliability_sentence
```

`majority` abstains on a real share of entity-years -- exactly the structural ceiling
`vignette("truth-fusion-case-study-midwifery")` documents for two-source panels, now showing up
on a four-source one too whenever the vote splits evenly. Where `crowd_kit` is available (not
guaranteed in every environment this vignette renders in -- see that chunk's `eval` guard), a
weighted method like `dawid_skene` can resolve those ties and report a *learned* reliability
ranking -- the real, verified version of this exact ranking (T-MSIS lowest, NPPES highest) is
in `docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md` S4, independently confirmed from the
`~/midwifery` session's own output files, not just asserted.

## What this vignette does and does not show

It shows eight genuinely distinct ways to compare sources without a gold standard, run end to
end on one coherent, internally-consistent simulated panel: direction and duration of timing,
pooled and covariate-stratified agreement, empirical staleness, churn independent of accuracy,
completeness against a defined universe, ecosystem convergence and lone-dissenter detection,
lineage-aware independence, and learned reliability under a forced choice. It shows that these
are not redundant: T-MSIS ranks worst on coverage, churn, convergence, *and* learned
reliability in this panel, but a sparse, low-coverage source (Open Payments) can still be
highly trusted on what it does cover -- a distinction only a convergence measure like
`attribute_source_corroboration()` surfaces, not coverage or churn alone.

It does **not** show real midwifery data. Every number above comes from a simulated panel,
seeded and calibrated to land near real, already-published findings
(`docs/midwifery-ablation-findings.md`, `docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md`) but never
claiming to reproduce them exactly -- real per-NPI data for this comparison lives outside this
package, by design, the same boundary every other midwifery-case-study doc and vignette in this
package observes. It does not establish which source is *correct* for any simulated or real
clinician -- no gold standard exists here either, by construction; every comparison above is
relative, the same honest limitation `docs/validation-protocol.md` documents for the real data.
